## Report

The claim that prolonged mask use causes dangerous CO2 buildup is not supported by mainstream scientific evidence for cloth or surgical masks worn by healthy people.

A peer-reviewed study in the *Annals of the American Thoracic Society* found that surgical masks and cloth face coverings do not meaningfully restrict oxygen intake or cause dangerous CO2 accumulation (https://www.aol.com/news/masks-not-restrict-oxygen-flow-134504166.html). This aligns with basic physics: CO2 molecules are small enough to diffuse freely through the porous fabric of cloth and surgical masks, and these masks are not airtight—unlike industrial respirators—so exhaled CO2 escapes rather than being trapped and rebreathed in physiologically significant amounts.

Fact-checking analyses (USA Today) reviewed the physiology and concluded it is "unlikely" that surgical or cloth masks cause hypoxia or hypercapnia in typical wearers, because these masks are looser-fitting than tight respirators (https://www.usatoday.com/story/news/factcheck/2020/05/30/fact-check-wearing-face-mask-not-cause-hypoxia-hypercapnia/5260106002/). Science-Based Medicine similarly reviewed these claims and found them "myths with no basis in physiology or chemistry" (https://sciencebasedmedicine.org/tag/hypercapnia/).

The strongest evidence against the blanket claim comes from tightly-fitted N95 respirators, not cloth/surgical masks: even here, clinical studies of patients with chronic hypercapnia using non-invasive ventilation found N95 and surgical masks did not significantly affect gas exchange (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41665923/). Some caution is warranted for vulnerable groups (infants, those with severe pre-existing respiratory disease) with tighter respirators, but for the general population wearing cloth/surgical masks, no dangerous CO2 buildup occurs.

**Conclusion:** Your skepticism is well-founded—the claim is false for cloth/surgical masks in the general population.
